title: Caffrey Darensbourg, the banjoist at the roof garden
summary: His favorite banjo player was his younger cousin Caffrey Darensbourg, a fast lead player at the roof garden who learned mandolin in their hometown first.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Speaking of banjo and guitar players, who were your favorites of the other musicians in the old days when you were starting out? Who did you like to listen to? Did you listen to some of the others when you weren't working? Did you ever go to here?
Did I listen to the other bands?
Yes. And which banjo players did you like?
Did I like to be your best? Yes. Which were the best players? Well, I will tell you. I had a little cousin. He was playing with P. Ron on the roof garden.
Oh, yeah.
I'd like to hear him play the band of your best. What was his name? His name was Catherine Darnsberg.
Oh, I've heard of him, yeah.
Boy, I was fast as lightning with his finger on the banjo.
George Geno told me about him. Has anyone went to Texas and got into some trouble somehow over there? Had a gambling place.
I and George Geno started to play in banjo just about the same year.
How did Caffrey play? Any special, like his solos or just musical chords?
Oh, yeah. What was his name? Oh, yeah. Solos and chords and picking his song out and everything.
Just a good all-round band.
He was, oh, yeah. He was up there with P. Ron in his outfit there. The roof garden. He had a roof garden. Right where that civic building is.
Yeah, I know. I know George Geno told me this is wonderful. He raves the band.
He was the owner of the fact. He was the owner of the city that played more lead on the banjo. And everybody started picking it up behind him.
Played the lead.
He played the lead and played cards and everything. About how old was he? Was he much older than you? No, I was about three years older than him. Oh, he was a young fellow.
Oh, yeah.
I was about three years older than him.

Somehow, you know, those people that are gone, we always think, well, they must be an old man. You know, they're older now. They're not here anymore. They must be an old-timer. They're younger than you then.
Yeah, are you? Mm-hmm.
I thought he was maybe an older man.
Yeah.
Do you know anything about where he learned to play or other bands that he worked with?
Where he learned to play?
Yes. Did he ever tell you?
Well, yeah, I can tell you that.
I could hear more about his life.
He learned to play a mandolin out in my hometown. That's his hometown, too. He moved that right.
I didn't know that.
He learned to play a mandolin there.
I don't know anything about it.
Yeah. And from the mandolin, he came over here in the city here.
Mm-hmm.

And why play in the mandolin so good here? And I guess some of the band publishers told him, says, why don't you buy your banjo? And I think you can do fine with it. So we ought to banjo and start with that.
